text.p: Australia's parliament on Monday began debating a move to quash the world's first voluntary euthanasia law, which has been strongly condemned by political, religious and community leaders.

As the debate opened a leading euthanasia campaigner said dying patients were lining up to use the law ahead of a parliamentary vote, and the son of the first man to die under the measure appealed for it to be kept.

Government backbencher Kevin Andrews, with Prime Minister John Howard's backing, has introduced a private bill which would require the government to use its constitutional powers to overturn the controversial law in the remote Northern Territory.
"This debate is about passing a bill that protects the vulnerable, or about leaving them exposed," Andrews told parliament, beginning what was expected to be a long debate.
"Territories do not have rights, they have responsibilities -- particularly to protect the ill and the vulnerable.
"If the parliament of the commonwealth of Australia cannot resolve a matter which goes to the life and death of its citizens, then what is the purpose of this parliament?"
Critics say Andrews' bill denies dying people control over their own life and overrides territory rights.

"It is dangerous in that it gives the parliamentarians in this place a position of moral superiority we do not and should not have," Christine Gallus, a fellow member of Andrews' Liberal Party, told the parliament.

The world's first assisted suicide law came into operation in the Northern Territory in July. But legal and political wrangles delayed its use until last month, when cancer patient Bob Dent became the first to die under the measure.
Dent's son, Rod, pleaded to national politicians not to overturn the law.

"I make a plea from my heart to all federal politicians on behalf of my father and all dying patients who want the right to choose voluntary euthanasia if their suffering becomes too great," he said in a statement from his home in Sydney.
The law has sparked an emotional debate throughout Australia, drawing criticism from civil leaders, church groups and the main doctors' body, the Australian Medical Association.
But opinion polls show an overwhelming majority of Australians -- about 75 percent -- support voluntary euthanasia.
The national parliament has the power to overturn laws in Australia's territories, but not the six states.

The doctor who helped Bob Dent die, leading euthanasia campaigner Philip Nitschke, said 11 terminally ill people had approached him to use the law before parliament votes on the Andrews bill, probably later this year.
A coalition of doctors, church and Aboriginal leaders has also launched a challenge in the Australian High Court, asking it to declare the territory legislation unconstitutional.
The Andrews bill, which is also backed by Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley, is expected to pass parliament's lower house, but its fate in the upper house Senate is uncertain.
